To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
activation of the phenlypropanoids pathway improves the performance of phloem- feeding insects by reducing the activity of the JA/ET pathway.
the phenylproponoid pathway in transgenic N. tabacum improves the performance of the whitefly, B. tabaci, by suppressing the jasmonate signaling.
the activation of the phenylethanolamine pathway in transgenic N. tabacum plants, which resulted in higher levels of flavone and flavonol accumulation, improved the fitness of the whitefly B. tabaci.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between the phenylproponoids pathway and phloem- feeding insects.

the effect of the activation of phenylpropanoic pathways on the performance of phloem- feeding insect, which may be important in the design of new strategies for the control of phloem feeding insects.
the interaction between the phenylprophanoids pathway, a major plant defensive pathway, and a phloem feeding insect model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the over-expression of the phenyl-propanoids pathway in transgenic tobacco does not improve the resistance to B. tabaci.

activation of the phenylethanoid pathway, which is a branch of the phenylalanine pathway, has a minor effect on whitefly performance and is not sufficient to overcome the negative effect of JA/ET-based defense on whitefly performance.
activation of the phenylethanol pathway has only a small negative effect on the fitness of B. tabaci, and that this negative effect is not sufficient for the insect to avoid the transgenic plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
activation of phenylpropanol biosynthesis pathway in plants, by over-expression PAP1 transcription factors, can be a successful way to improve the fitness of phloem- feeding insects.
activation of the phenolpropanoid pathway improves the performance of B. tabaci on transgenic plants via reduced JA/ET signaling.
the activation of the phenolic pathway in N. tabacum improves the performance of the whitefly B. tabaci by suppressing JA signaling in the host plants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phenylproponoid pathway, when activated, is a major source for the accumulation of SA, a hormone that can suppress the plant's defenses against B. tabaci.
the activation of the phenypropanoids pathway does not improve plant defense against B. tabaci, which may have important implications for the utilization of this defense pathway in transgenic crops.
the activation of the phenolic pathway in transgenic tobacco plants does not affect the performance of B. tabaci.
